title: How Mary Peltola Won Alaska
author: Youth Outsider Editorial Team
dek: Two weeks after Election Day, the last Senate race of 2026 went to a Yup'ik fisherwoman from the Kuskokwim River. She will be Alaska's first Alaska Native senator.
cover_alt: Collage of Mary Peltola, a map of Alaska and the Kuskokwim River
cover_caption: Collage by Youth Outsider. Photos: House Creative Services (public domain); Joseph from Cabin On The Road (CC BY-SA 2.0); map: Nzeemin (CC BY-SA 3.0).

figures.alt: The Kuskokwim River in Southwest Alaska

body:
The last Senate race of the 2026 midterms is over. On Tuesday night, two weeks after Election Day, the Associated Press called Alaska's Senate race for Democrat Mary Peltola, who unseated two-term Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan. As of Wednesday morning, AP's count had Peltola at 50.1% and Sullivan at 45.8%, [Time reported](https://time.com/article/2026/11/18/democrat-mary-peltola-wins-alaska-senate-race/).

Her win makes history several times over. Peltola, who is Yup'ik, will be the first Alaska Native ever elected to the U.S. Senate, and the first Democrat Alaska has sent to the Senate since 2008. It also gives Democrats a 56-44 majority. They flipped nine Senate seats this year, the most for either party since 1958, [according to the AP](https://abc7ny.com/post/alaska-senate-race-2026-update-democrat-mary-peltola-wins-election-beating-incumbent-republican-dan-sullivan/20049828/).

*"As a lifelong Alaskan who has dedicated my life to serving our state, there is no greater honor than having Alaskans' support,"* Peltola said in a statement, [CBS News reported](https://www.cbsnews.com/news/alaska-2026-senate-sullivan-peltola/). She promised to *"take on corporate greed, lower costs, and put Alaska first,"* and ended with *"Thank you Alaska. Let's get to work."*

Peltola, 53, grew up fishing with her family along the Kuskokwim River in Southwest Alaska and was captaining her own boat by 14, [according to Native News Online](https://nativenewsonline.net/currents/breaking-news-mary-peltola-yupik-wins-senate-seat-in-alaska/). She worked as a salmon and herring technician for the state, ran an intertribal commission that manages the river's salmon, and served 10 years in the Alaska House. In 2022, after Rep. Don Young died, she won the state's only House seat, beating Sarah Palin to become the first Alaska Native member of Congress. She lost that seat in 2024 to Republican Nick Begich III by less than three points, in a year when Donald Trump carried Alaska by 13.

She launched her Senate campaign in January and built it around the cost of living. In a state where many towns can only be reached by plane or boat, fuel, food and heating are expensive even in good years. This year they got worse. Gas and diesel prices rose with the war in Iran, and Peltola went after Sullivan for supporting the war, tying it directly to what Alaskans were paying for fuel. More than 80% of Alaska voters told exit pollsters they were worried about the price of necessities like gas, food, utilities and health care, Time reported.

She also ran as an Alaskan first. Both candidates accused each other of putting "Lower 48" interests ahead of the state's, and Peltola promised she would never put *"any Lower 48 politician before Alaskans."* On data centers, which Sullivan has pushed to build on military bases, she said she would let local communities decide, as long as the projects don't raise power costs for everyone else. Her platform stuck close to home: fisheries, affordable energy, the cost of living, veterans and political reform.

The national mood helped too. The Iran war and high gas prices weighed on Republicans across the country, and polls showed the Alaska race as a dead heat going into Election Day. Republicans sent Vice President JD Vance to campaign for Sullivan, and the Senate Leadership Fund, the main Republican Senate super PAC, spent heavily to save him. It was not enough.

The race was also one of the strangest of the year. In June, a former Petersburg teacher named Dan J. Sullivan, with almost the same name as the senator, entered the race and finished third in the open primary, which put him on the November ballot. Republicans accused Peltola's campaign of helping recruit him to confuse voters, a charge she denied, calling it *"just another distraction."* The Trump administration sued to block the state from certifying a Peltola win. A federal judge dismissed the suit, and the Justice Department is appealing and has opened a criminal investigation. On Election Day, the senator called it *"the biggest election cheating scandal"* in Alaska's history. CBS News reported that Peltola's margin was large enough that votes for the other Sullivan would not have changed the outcome.

The fight may not be over. Sullivan's campaign has said it will not concede until the race is certified, which the state is aiming to do by Nov. 25, and Trump called the race a *"disgrace"* on Monday, [according to Democracy Docket](https://www.democracydocket.com/news-alerts/live-updates-alaska-senate-race-set-for-democratic-win-with-gop-set-to-fight-results/).

Alaska also elected Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins as governor, the party's first win for that office there since 1998. And when the new Senate is sworn in on Jan. 3, Peltola will take office alongside Minnesota's Peggy Flanagan. They will be the first two Native women ever to serve in the Senate.
